A free template is included so you can get started immediately. What is a social media calendar? A social media calendar is a forward-looking plan of all scheduled posts across your social media platforms, organized by publish date, time and network. It captures every element of a post, including copy, links, tags, @-mentions and media like images and video, so your team publishes with precision and consistency. Unlike a general content calendar, which maps all marketing content across every channel, a social media calendar focuses specifically on social: what goes out, where it goes and who owns every step of the process. You can build one using a spreadsheet, a digital calendar or a social media management platform like Sprout Social, which gives you an interactive publishing dashboard, post scheduling and team collaboration in one place. The core benefits include saving time, maintaining a consistent posting schedule, protecting brand quality, streamlining approvals, supporting campaign planning, enabling content repurposing and improving performance tracking. 1. Saves time and widens team bandwidth Planning core content ahead of time reduces the daily scramble while leaving room for timely, reactive posts. This eliminates the rush for ideas and frees your team to focus on what moves the needle: creating high-quality content and testing strategies that resonate with your audience. Teams align around key deadlines and campaigns, messaging stays cohesive across departments and last-minute scrambles disappear. 5. Core fields every social media content calendar needs Track the details that keep publishing organized and your team aligned across every post and platform. Publish date: The day the post goes live. Publish time: The exact time the post is scheduled. Platform: The social media platform the post is built for. Post format: Reel, carousel, video, image, Story, text post or another format. Caption or copy: The final approved message. Creative asset: The image, video or design attached to the post. Link and CTA: The destination URL and the action you want people to take. Campaign or content pillar: The theme, initiative or launch the post supports. Owner: The person responsible for creating, reviewing or publishing the post. Status: Draft, in review, approved, scheduled or published. Approval notes: Feedback, edits or legal and brand guidance tied to the post. Tags: Labels that support sorting and reporting on content later. A balanced mix keeps your feed engaging and supports your content marketing goals. Set a posting schedule. Decide how often to post on each platform and when your audience is most active. It’s better to be consistent than to post a lot, so pick a schedule you can stick with. Map posts around campaign dates, and leave enough time for writing, design, review, and changes before you publish. Keep a library of evergreen ideas. Save evergreen post ideas, such as tips, how-tos, and customer questions, in a separate section of your calendar. Pull from it when a timely post falls through, or the schedule has a gap. Organize your content in a shared platform. A content calendar centralizes your schedule, lets your team see upcoming work, track progress, and collaborate on content in real time. Review, refine, and repeat. After publishing, monitor engagement metrics and update your calendar based on results. Continuously improve your social media calendar as you learn what works best. A pre-built template lets you start planning immediately. Asana’s free social media calendar template provides a framework for organizing posts and collaborating with contributors. Assign responsibilities for preparation, review, and publishing, then add the details your team needs. Read: Free social media reporting template that saves hours of your time How do I use Asana's social media calendar template? Create a new project by copying Asana’s social media calendar template, then enter your team’s details. Invite social media managers, content creators, and reviewers who will contribute to each post. Let’s follow a small marketing team launching a product: Maya manages social media, Leo designs assets, and Priya reviews posts. This example demonstrates how they plan a week of content, implement changes before publishing, and use results to inform future actions. 1. Copy the template and set the campaign goal Open the template page , select Use template, and sign up to begin. Name the project clearly for your team, and document the campaign objectives before adding posts to the calendar. Maya names the campaign “Product launch” and sets a goal of 100 visits to the launch page during launch week. She’ll use tagged links in the social posts and check visits in web analytics. Recording that goal gives Leo and Priya context for the assets they create and review. For teams receiving lots of content requests, AI Studio can help check whether a brief has the information needed to start work. You could build a workflow that checks for the channel, objective, asset link, and reviewer, then asks for missing details or sends the request to the right person. COS uses AI Studio to check incoming briefs with project-manager oversight. The company reports a 90% reduction in campaign setup time across its broader AI workflow. A person still reviews the request and approves the final content. 2. Add posts and publishing slots Create a separate task for each post, specifying its channel, format, copy, and images or video. Maya plans a mix of teasers, launch announcements, and follow-up content to give the audience varied reasons to visit the launch page. This sample social media calendar outlines the team’s plan as of Monday’s review. Post Channel + format Review date Publish slot Status Teaser reel Instagram reel Fri 15:00 Mon 10:00 Approved Launch carousel Instagram carousel Mon 15:00 Tue 10:00 Needs revision Launch announcement LinkedIn post Mon 16:00 Tue 11:00 Approved Feature demo Instagram video Tue 15:00 Wed 10:00 In design Customer Q&A Instagram Q&A Thu 15:00 Fri 11:00 Planned Copy the blank version below to plan your social media marketing schedule. Add a row for each post and allocate time for revisions between the review deadline and publishing slot. Post Channel + format Review due Publish slot Status Include the remaining details in each post’s task to ensure contributors have all necessary information: Campaign and goal: The campaign name and what the post should help achieve. People: The post owner, reviewer, and publisher. Content: The caption, asset links, destination URL, hashtags, and mentions. Results: The live-post link, metric, data source, review date, and next action. Set each post task’s due date to its planned publishing day so it appears in Calendar view . Record the publishing time and time zone within the task. Use status indicators such as Planned, In design, Needs revision, Approved, and Published to track progress, either in task details or a custom field. 3. Assign owners and production deadlines Assign each post an owner responsible for overseeing it through publication. Maya owns the five post tasks, delegating a subtask for assets to Leo and a review subtask for Priya, each with a deadline before the scheduled publishing date. Maintain copy, asset links, and feedback within the post task. When Leo uploads a design, he notifies Priya that it is ready for review. If Priya requests changes, she documents them next to the asset and assigns the next step. This process lets the team keep working without waiting for meetings or searching through separate conversations. In the same State of Marketing Collaboration study, 23% of marketing professionals said their organization's goals and objectives are spread across too many places. Document decisions and next steps within the task so colleagues have the context they need to respond when available. 4. Review and revise before approval Agree on review criteria before approving a post. Priya checks that the copy supports the campaign goal, the asset fits the channel, and the link reaches the launch page. On Monday, she spots a missing launch link in Carousel v2, comments on the change, and keeps the status at “Needs revision.” Leo uploads Carousel v3 by 13:00 so Priya can review it by 15:00. Once she approves it, Maya marks the post “Approved,” keeping the final copy, asset, and approval together for publishing. Start with comments and review subtasks, then add built-in Approvals and Rules as needed. If the review runs late, Maya moves the publishing slot and tells contributors. When rescheduling in Calendar view, update the publishing time and any affected production or review deadlines. 5. Hand approved posts off for publishing Before scheduling a post in the publishing platform, Maya verifies the approved copy, final asset, channel, link, and time zone. Once the post is live, she adds the live-post link to the task and updates the status to “Published.” If your team uses Hootsuite , the integration lets you access Asana tasks in Hootsuite Plan and select content for publishing. Completing an Asana task or changing its date does not automatically publish a post; a team member must still schedule or publish the approved content. 6. Review results and plan the next posts Choose someone to review performance and put the review date on the calendar. Agreeing on the goal, metric, and person responsible gives the team a shared basis for deciding what to change. The following Monday, Maya checks tagged launch-page visits for the campaign. In this example, the posts brought in 80 visits against the 100-visit goal. She records the result and measurement period, then checks link clicks and landing-page behavior to investigate the shortfall. For the next campaign, she could test a more specific call to action. Reviewing social media metrics helps the team decide what to repeat, improve, or change in the next week’s content. How teams use Asana for social media planning With Asana’s social media calendar template, you can plan upcoming posts and manage related work in one place. Benefits include visibility into scheduled content and support for contributors as they prepare, review, and deliver posts. The following examples illustrate how teams use Asana’s planning tools effectively. CityFibre brings requests and approvals into one campaign View planned campaigns alongside incoming requests to determine where new work fits and who should review it. CityFibre consolidates campaigns, social posts, ad-hoc requests, and press releases into a single social media calendar, with approval processes to ensure proper sign-offs before publishing. Keeping the request, owner, and review decision together helps your team identify which posts are ready and which require further attention. Read CityFibre’s case study → Montblanc connects social posts with the wider campaign Align your social content with your marketing plan and share your calendar with stakeholders on related channels. Montblanc uses its communications calendar to coordinate monthly Instagram content, CRM newsletters, e-commerce activities, and external agencies. This shared view enables teams to plan campaign steps collaboratively. If a launch date changes, the social team can review teasers and announcements alongside other campaign activities. Read Montblanc’s case study → Discovery integrates its social calendar with production A calendar is more useful when it reflects the current status of content. At Discovery Digital Studios, a publishing task appears in both the video production project and the Instagram content calendar. Updates, comments, and completion status stay in sync because it is the same task. Your team can adopt this approach to keep copy, assets, and feedback consolidated while providing relevant teams with visibility into the work that matters to them. Read Discovery’s case study → The NCAA reuses production steps for social content Once you establish a process for a recurring post format, save the steps so future posts follow the same preparation and review requirements. The NCAA uses task templates for social posts and infographics, subtasks to divide production work, and forms to collect content submissions . Repeating this structure helps contributors understand expectations and next steps, while allowing flexibility to adapt content for each campaign. These tools increase visibility for your social media team and minimize disruptions from switching between applications. Integrated features Calendar View. View all upcoming and past work in a calendar format to track deadlines at a glance. Click any task to access custom fields, dependencies, subtasks, and additional details. Custom fields. Tag, sort, and filter work using custom fields for any information you need to track, such as status or platform. Share custom fields across tasks and projects to maintain consistency throughout your organization. Subtasks. Divide larger tasks into smaller components while maintaining their connection to the parent task. This is particularly useful when a post requires multiple contributors or approval steps before publication. Dependencies. Indicate when a task depends on another so your team knows when work is blocked and when to start. For example, link a review task to the design work it requires so the reviewer can see what must be completed first. Select features that match your team’s needs and review your plan . The Personal plan supports two users; larger teams require a paid plan. Custom fields, automations, and dependencies are available with Starter or higher, while built-in Approvals and proofing require Advanced or higher. AI Studio is included in the Starter, Advanced, and Enterprise plans, subject to admin enablement and usage limits. Recommended apps Figma. Teams use Figma to create user flows, wireframes, UI mocks, prototypes, and more. You can now embed these designs in Asana, allowing your team to reference the latest design work alongside related project documents. Unlike screenshots, live embeds update in real time to reflect changes, so you don't have to locate and update files manually. HubSpot. Automatically create Asana tasks using HubSpot Workflows. Leverage customer data in HubSpot CRM to automate processes. For example, use the integration to convert a campaign follow-up into an Asana task and assign it to the appropriate team member. Hootsuite. Access Asana tasks within Hootsuite Plan and select approved content when ready to schedule. Your team can prepare and review posts in Asana, then manage publishing through Hootsuite. Get started with your social media calendar A well-organized social media calendar helps your team stay on track, collaborate efficiently, and ensure every post supports your broader marketing goals. Plan ahead, monitor performance, and adjust your strategy based on real data instead of relying on last-minute ideas. Free social media calendar template FAQs about social media calendar templates How do I create a social media calendar? Start by defining your goals, choosing the right platforms, and mapping out a content mix and posting schedule. For each post, record the owner, copy and assets, review deadline, and publishing time. Keep those details in a shared social content calendar so contributors can see what they need to prepare and when. Is there a free social media scheduling tool? Yes, Asana offers a free social media calendar template to organize posts, assign work, and track dates. The free Personal plan supports two people; larger teams and features such as custom fields, rules, and Approvals require a paid plan. Check Asana’s plans for the features you need. The calendar helps you prepare posts; publishing happens through your social channels or publishing software. What is the difference between a content calendar template and a social media content calendar template? A content calendar template covers all content types, including blogs, videos, and emails, while a social media content calendar template focuses specifically on scheduling and managing posts for social platforms. Both help ensure consistency, but the social media version is tailored for platform-specific strategies and engagement. What features should you look for in a social media content calendar template? Look for customizable fields for post details like captions, publish dates, platforms, and content types, along with tracking for post status, approvals, and performance metrics. These features help you plan, run, and analyze your social media campaigns from one place. Can you use a content calendar template as a social media content planner? Yes, you can adapt a general content calendar template into a social media content planner by adding platform-specific details like post dates, captions, visuals, and channel selection. This approach lets you manage all your content planning in one place. How far in advance should I plan my social media calendar? Plan far enough ahead to write the posts, create the assets, complete reviews, and make changes before publishing. Put major campaigns and launch dates on the calendar first, then work backward to set production deadlines. Leave room for timely posts and review the schedule regularly. The right planning period depends on your team’s capacity and review process. What is a social media calendar? A social media calendar is a shared schedule of planned posts across your social channels. For each post, it records the platform, format, copy, assets, publishing date and time, owner, and status. Teams use it to maintain consistent posting, link posts to campaign goals, and give everyone a clear view of upcoming work. Why is a social media content calendar important? A social media content calendar helps your team post consistently and plan around campaign dates instead of coming up with ideas at the last minute. It shows who owns each post, when reviews are due, and what is ready to publish. That shared view reduces missed deadlines and makes it easier to see which posts support your goals.
